kernels.definition: By the law of supply, a higher price raises the quantity producers are willing to supply, so the supply curve slopes upward.

definitionAnchor.quote: a higher price raises the quantity that producers are willing to supply, so the supply curve slopes upward

facts.text: A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve, while a change in input costs or technology shifts the whole curve.

anchor.quote: A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve, while a change in input costs or technology shifts the whole curve

facts.text: Quantity supplied is a flow per period, not a fixed stock.

anchor.quote: Quantity supplied is a flow per period, not a fixed stock

kernels.definition: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost, even if another producer is better at making everything.

definitionAnchor.quote: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost

facts.text: When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.

anchor.quote: When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises

facts.text: Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill.

anchor.quote: Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill

kernels.definition: An externality is a cost or benefit from a transaction that falls on a third party who is not part of the exchange.

definitionAnchor.quote: An externality is a cost or benefit from a transaction that falls on a third party who is not part of the exchange

facts.text: With a negative externality like pollution, the market produces more than the socially efficient quantity because the price excludes the spillover cost.

anchor.quote: the market produces more than the socially efficient quantity because the price excludes the spillover cost

facts.text: Correcting an externality means making decision-makers face the costs or benefits the market boundary leaves out.

anchor.quote: making the decision-makers face the costs or benefits the market boundary leaves out

kernels.definition: A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.

definitionAnchor.quote: a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry

facts.text: Unlike a price-taking competitive firm, a monopoly is a price maker: it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells.

anchor.quote: a monopoly is a price maker: it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells

facts.text: Because it produces less and charges more than a competitive market, a monopoly creates deadweight loss.

mcItems.q: If the price of a good increases, what happens to the quantity producers are willing to supply?
op: The quantity supplied decreases
The quantity supplied remains unchanged
The quantity supplied increases
The quantity supplied shifts the entire curve
mcItems.ex: Quantity supplied is a flow per period, not a fixed stock. The quantity supplied increases because a higher price raises the quantity producers are willing to supply.

mcItems.q: What causes a movement along the supply curve?
op: A change in input costs or technology
A change in the good's own price
A shift in the entire curve
A change in the good's own price
mcItems.ex: A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve. A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve.

keyTerms.df: The line illustrating the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity producers are willing to offer for sale.
keyTerms.eg: If the price of wheat rises, farmers will offer a larger quantity of wheat for sale.
keyTerms.mi: The supply curve represents the total amount of a good that exists in the market at a specific price point.
keyTerms.cx: The supply curve shows how the quantity producers are willing to supply changes when the good's own price changes.

keyTerms.df: A change in factors other than the good's own price that alters the entire supply curve.
keyTerms.eg: If the cost of labor decreases, the entire supply curve shifts to the right.
keyTerms.mi: A supply shift is the same as a movement along the supply curve caused by a change in the good's own price.
keyTerms.cx: A supply shift occurs when input costs or technology change, moving the whole curve.

mcItems.q: A producer possesses a comparative advantage in producing a good when they can create it at which lower opportunity cost?
op: The producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost.
The producer has an absolute advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost.
The producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost,
The producer has an absolute advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost.
mcItems.ex: The producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost.

mcItems.q: When producers specialize based on comparative advantage and then engage in trade, what is the resulting effect on total output and consumption levels?
op: Total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.
Total output remains the same, but both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.
Total output rises, but neither producer can consume beyond what they could produce alone.
Total output remains the same, and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.
mcItems.ex: Total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.

keyTerms.df: This describes the situation where one entity can produce a good using fewer resources than another entity.
keyTerms.eg: If Producer A can make 10 widgets for the same resources that Producer B can only make 5 widgets, Producer A has the relative cost advantage.
keyTerms.mi: The relative cost advantage is determined solely by the total quantity of output each producer can generate.
keyTerms.cx: The relative cost advantage is determined by the opportunity cost associated with producing each good.

keyTerms.df: This involves producers focusing their production efforts on the good where they have the lowest opportunity cost.
keyTerms.eg: If Producer X has a lower opportunity cost for making chairs than Producer Y, Producer X should specialize in chairs.
keyTerms.mi: Specialization based on comparative advantage is the process where producers focus on the good they can make at the lower opportunity cost.
keyTerms.cx: Specialization based on comparative advantage is the process where producers focus on the good they can make at the lower opportunity cost.

mcItems.q: When a negative externality exists, what is the typical market outcome compared to the socially efficient quantity?
op: The market produces the socially efficient quantity because the price incorporates the spill-on
The market produces more than the socially efficient quantity because the price excludes the sp
The market produces less than the socially efficient quantity because the price includes the sp
The market produces the socially efficient quantity because the price incorporates the sp
mcItems.ex: The market produces more than the socially efficient quantity because the price excludes the spillover cost. The most plausible misconception is that the market outcome is always the socially efficient quantity, which is incorrect when negative externalities are present.

mcItems.q: What action is required to correct an externality?
op: Adjusting the firm's production level to match the social cost
Making decision-makers face the costs or benefits the market boundary leaves out
Increasing the price to reflect the full social cost of the transaction
Allowing the market to self-correct by increasing the quantity produced
mcItems.ex: Correcting an externality means making decision-makers face the costs or benefits the market boundary leaves out. The most plausible misconception is that correcting an externality only involves adjusting the firm's production level, which ignores the broader scope of the correction.

keyTerms.tr: Cost or benefit from a transaction falling on a third party
keyTerms.df: This is a cost or benefit from a transaction that falls on a third party who is not part of the exchange.
keyTerms.eg: When a factory pollutes a nearby river, the cost of the pollution falls on the local community who do not participate in the factory's transaction.
keyTerms.mi: This term refers to the internal cost incurred by the producer of a good.
keyTerms.cx: This concept describes an external cost or benefit that affects someone outside the direct trade.

keyTerms.df: Market power is distinct from firm size; it relates to the ability of a firm to influence market prices.
keyTerms.eg: A small firm with a unique technology can have significant market power even if its size is small.
keyTerms.mi: This term is synonymous with the physical scale or number of units a business produces.
keyTerms.cx: This concept describes the degree to which a single entity can control the price of a good or service in a market.

Private cost

mcItems.q: What economic consequence arises when a single seller produces less and charges a higher price than a competitive market?
op: Deadweight loss
Absolute advantage
Comparative advantage
Private cost
mcItems.ex: Because it produces less and charges more than a competitive market, a monopoly creates deadweight loss.

keyTerms.df: A market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.
keyTerms.eg: A local utility company providing water to a city is a monopoly.
keyTerms.mi: A monopoly is a price taker.
keyTerms.cx: A monopoly is a price maker because it can raise the price by restricting the quantity it sells.

keyTerms.df: Unlike a price-taking competitive firm, a monopoly is a price maker: it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells.
keyTerms.eg: A firm with a monopoly can increase its selling price by reducing the amount of goods it offers.
keyTerms.mi: A price maker is a firm that cannot change its price.
keyTerms.cx: A price maker is a firm that can raise its price by restricting the quantity it sells.
